paper_name: Differentiable Neural Surface Refinement for Modeling Transparent Objects

sections.abstract: Neural implicit surface reconstruction using volume rendering performs poorly for transparent objects because standard functions do not account for refraction and reflection. This paper introduces Transparent Neural Surface Refinement (TNSR), a framework that explicitly incorporates physical refraction and reflection tracing. A key contribution is a differentiable technique that allows photometric signals to propagate back to the surface model, enabling end-to-end optimization using only multi-view RGB images and significantly improving geometry estimation.
sections.introduction: Neural implicit representations usually assume linear light paths, failing for refractive materials like glass. Reconstructing these objects typically requires complex, controlled setups. TNSR addresses this by using color consistency and a learned background model to compute reflected and refracted rays via sphere tracing and Snell’s Law. The method is fully differentiable, allowing error signals to update implicit surface parameters via a nested optimization strategy.
sections.method: TNSR builds on neural implicit surfaces like NeuS, representing geometry as an SDF $\phi_{\text{SDF}} : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ and appearance as $\phi_{\text{color}}$. It addresses limitations in existing work—such as the straight-line light transport assumption in VolSDF or the need for controlled setups in traditional transparent reconstruction—by using color consistency. Volume rendering is performed via: $\hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{d}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \alpha_i \mathbf{c}_i \prod_{j=1}^{i-1}(1-\alpha_j)$ (1), where opacity $\alpha_i$ is derived from the SDF: $\alpha_i = \max \left \{ \frac{\Phi_s(\phi_{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}_i))- \Phi_s(\phi_{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}_{i+1}))}{\Phi_s(\phi_{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}_i))},\, 0 \right \} (2)$. Losses include a photometric loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{c}}$ (Eq 3), an Eikonal loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{e}}$ (Eq 4), and a normal smoothness loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{n}}$ (Eq 6). The method refines surfaces by tracing reflected rays $\mathbf{d}_{1}^r = \mathbf{d}_0 - 2(\mathbf{n}_1^\top \mathbf{d}_0)\mathbf{n}_1$ (8) and refracted rays $\mathbf{d}_1 = \frac{\eta}{\eta_{t}} \mathbf{d}_0 - \left ( \frac{\eta}{\eta_{t}} \mathbf{n}_1^\top \mathbf{d}_0 + \sqrt{1 - \frac{\eta^2}{\eta_{t}^2} \left ( 1 - (\mathbf{n}_1^\top \mathbf{d}_0)^2 \right )} \right ) \mathbf{n}_1$ (9). Final radiance is: $\hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{d}_0) = F_r \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{d}_1^r) + (1 - F_r) \hat{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{x}_2, \mathbf{d}_2)$ (11). To enable backpropagation, surface distance $\delta_i$ is treated as an optimization: $\delta_{i}(\boldsymbol{\theta}, \mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{d}_i) \in \text{argmin}_{\delta \geqslant \epsilon} \delta$ subject to $\phi_{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}_i + \delta \mathbf{d}_i; \boldsymbol{\theta}) = 0$ (12). Analytical derivatives are: $\frac{d\delta_i}{d\boldsymbol{\theta}} = -\frac{1}{\mathbf{n}_{i+1}^\top \mathbf{d}_i} \frac{\partial}{\partial \boldsymbol{\theta}}\phi_{\text{SDF}}(\mathbf{x}_{i+1}; \boldsymbol{\theta})$ (13), $\frac{d\delta_i}{d\mathbf{x}_i} = -\frac{\mathbf{n}_{i+1}}{\mathbf{n}_{i+1}^\top \mathbf{d}_i}$ (14), and $\frac{d\delta_i}{d\mathbf{d}_i} = -\frac{\delta_i \mathbf{n}_{i+1}}{\mathbf{n}_{i+1}^\top \mathbf{d}_i}$ (15).
sections.experiments: The framework was evaluated using real-world datasets (Glass, Ball) and synthetic models (Kitty, Optical Ball, Bottle, Ellipsoid). Baselines included standard NeRF implementations (TensoRF, Instant-NGP, Nerfacto) and specialized refraction methods such as MS-NeRF and Eikonal Fields.
